title: Why Use Textplot?
description: Textplot renders ASCII and Unicode charts as `VARCHAR` values right inside a `SELECT`. The point: when you're poking at data in the [DuckDB CLI](https://duckdb.org/docs/api/cli/overview), you can see the shape of a distribution, the trend of a series, or the level of a metric without copying numbers into a notebook or a BI tool. Quick eyeballing — not a replacement for real visualization when you actually need axes, hover, or pixels.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: Inline visuals for terminal-first SQL workflows. The output is plain text, so it travels through `.mode line`, log files, status emails, and READMEs the same way any other column does.

bulletPoints.label: Eyeballing distributions
bulletPoints.description: Wrap an aggregate in [`tp_density`](#tp_density) to see whether a column is roughly normal, bimodal, or has a long tail — in one row of CLI output, no matplotlib round-trip.

bulletPoints.label: Per-row trend cells
bulletPoints.description: Drop a [`tp_sparkline`](#tp_sparkline) into a `SELECT` list against a table where each row carries an array of values; you get one sparkline per entity in the result table.

bulletPoints.label: Status indicators
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_bar`](#tp_bar) with threshold-based coloring is the natural shape for SLA / disk / health columns in a fleet table.

bulletPoints.label: Scannable links
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_qr`](#tp_qr) renders a QR code as Unicode blocks for embedding in terminal output, dashboards, or docs.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: Every function returns a `VARCHAR` — there's no client-side renderer, no asset pipeline, no extra dependency in the query plan. Each function takes a positional value (or array) plus a small set of named parameters for width, style, and characters.

bulletPoints.label: Charts as strings
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_bar`](#tp_bar), [`tp_sparkline`](#tp_sparkline), and [`tp_density`](#tp_density) all return a single `VARCHAR` cell. Width is parameterized so columns line up across rows.

bulletPoints.label: Named-parameter styling
bulletPoints.description: `shape`, `style`, `theme`, `width`, `on_color`, `off_color`, and `thresholds` are all passed via DuckDB's [named-parameter syntax](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/overview#named-parameters). `on` and `off` collide with SQL keywords — quote them as `"on"` and `"off"`.

bulletPoints.label: Three sparkline modes
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_sparkline`](#tp_sparkline) picks a vocabulary based on `mode`: `absolute` (height ∝ value), `delta` (direction of change), or `trend` (signed magnitude). Each mode has multiple themes — blocks, arrows, faces, slopes.

bulletPoints.label: Density plot styles
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_density`](#tp_density) ships several character-set styles — `shaded`, `ascii`, `dots`, `height`, `circles`, `rainbow_circle` — so you can pick one that fits the output medium (terminal, email, README).

sections.title: What it isn't
sections.description: Textplot is a CLI ergonomics tool. It earns its place when the alternative is squinting at numbers — not when you actually need a real chart.

bulletPoints.label: Not a visualization library
bulletPoints.description: Character-grid resolution caps detail. For interactive dashboards, publication figures, or anything where pixels matter, use a real charting tool — [Matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/), [Vega-Lite](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/), [Observable Plot](https://observablehq.com/plot), [Apache Superset](https://superset.apache.org/), etc.

bulletPoints.label: Not a statistical summary
bulletPoints.description: [`tp_density`](#tp_density) shows the shape of a distribution; it doesn't compute moments, fit kernels, or give you confidence intervals. Pair it with `quantile_cont`, `stddev_pop`, or [`datasketches`](/products/extensions/datasketches) when you need numbers.

bulletPoints.label: Unicode rendering varies
bulletPoints.description: Emoji and block characters depend on the terminal font. For maximum portability use `style := 'ascii'` (`tp_density`), `theme := 'ascii_basic'` (`tp_sparkline`), or custom `"on"` / `"off"` characters with [`tp_bar`](#tp_bar) and [`tp_qr`](#tp_qr).

useCases.title: See the shape of a column inline
useCases.description: `SELECT tp_density(array_agg(value)) FROM measurements;` — one row of CLI output that tells you whether the data is roughly normal, bimodal, or skewed, without leaving SQL.

useCases.title: Sparklines per row in a status table
useCases.description: Pre-aggregate a series per entity into an array column, then render [`tp_sparkline`](#tp_sparkline) in the `SELECT`. You get a fleet view that fits in a terminal window.

useCases.title: Threshold-colored health bars
useCases.description: [`tp_bar`](#tp_bar) with a `thresholds` list is the classic SLA / disk-utilization / risk indicator. Sort by the underlying number; let the bar carry the visual.

useCases.title: Embed scannable links
useCases.description: [`tp_qr`](#tp_qr) renders Unicode-block QR codes for terminal output, status emails, and README embeds. `ecc := 'high'` for tolerant rendering, custom characters for styling.
